title: Spearhead: new trailer for my WW2 eastern front RTS where you can also jump into the gunner seat
author: greenlight91
selftext:
edit: sorry, I missed rule 4. here is how I made it.



I'm a solo dev in Korea. almost all of the C# code is written by Claude Code inside my Unity 6 project, and my part is the design, direction and testing. I explain what I want in Korean, it writes the code, I play the build and send back screenshots or short clips of what looks wrong, and we repeat that loop many times a day. bigger features go through a plan and a mockup image first and I approve it before anything gets built, because when I let it build straight from a description the result was often not what I imagined. sometimes I run a few agents at the same time, one plans and the others build different parts.



the part I'm most proud of is the armor system. every tank has armor plates with real thickness and angle from historical data, and each shell is checked against the plate it actually hits, so there is no hp bar for tanks. the AI wrote that code, but I spent a lot of time testing it shot by shot until penetration felt right.



for assets, most 3D models are bought asset packs, and some small props and weapons were made with Blender python scripts that Claude wrote. voices are ElevenLabs, the music in this trailer is Suno, and the key art is temporary AI art that I want to replace before release, same for the sound effects. this trailer was also cut with ffmpeg scripts it wrote, including the captions and their small animations.



what I learned: the AI is very confident even when it is wrong, so I always check the result myself. just today it told me my flamethrower model was white because the texture was missing, but the real reason was that Unity never extracted the texture embedded in the fbx. also in a big project it starts to lose track, so I keep a code map document and memory notes so every new session knows where things are.



happy to answer questions about the workflow.
